content: 1. Education and training interventions, when implemented in isolation, are rarely evaluated in terms of their impact on surgical site infection (SSI) rates. Typically, these interventions are combined with specific technical changes to enhance their effectiveness. 2. Examples of improvement interventions for reducing SSIs include: Implementing automatic stop orders to prevent the continuation of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP) after the procedure. For instance, one study estimated that approximately 600 hours of staff time were dedicated to meetings for the development, implementation, and evaluation of an antibiotic prophylaxis policy. Transitioning from paper wraps to metal containers for surgical instrument sets, as well as improving postoperative care of surgical wounds. Establishing a policy for pre-approval of immediate and rapid processing in the sterile processing department. Developing a manual for equipment cleaning resources. Introducing a rapid sterilization hand-off communication tool. 3. Practical examples of specific interventions include: Changing vendor contracts to ensure surgical instruments are delivered 48 hours before surgery, with penalty clauses for breaches of contract. Placing stickers on surgical dressings with contact information and instructions for addressing concerns about dressing integrity or contamination. Engaging attending physicians or surgeons to directly observe and confirm the execution of improved skin preparation protocols. Making preoperative telephone calls to patients to remind them to begin manual bowel preparation with oral antibiotics and to perform preoperative bathing. 4. Key elements for successful execution of SSI prevention strategies include: Protocols, pathways, and policies aimed at frontline staff to clearly delineate information and facilitate the implementation of evidence-based recommendations. Bundling care processes to standardize key interventions, making them easier to execute. Utilizing checklists as tools to improve the quality of care. Implementing order sets, electronic reminders, and automatic stops for antibiotics as long-term, facility-wide initiatives to ensure consistent care. Employing safety and quality improvement models to enable stepwise implementation and rapid identification of inefficiencies in processes. 5. Regular evaluation of performance measures and unintended consequences is essential for monitoring progress against care processes and outcomes. This should involve timely feedback to ensure continuous improvement. 6. Evaluation methods that have proven effective include: Direct observation of processes by senior nurses or physicians. Combined chart audits and direct observations to measure compliance with recommended measures, such as preoperative preparation. Targeted monitoring, auditing, and evaluation tools, such as surgical auditing tools, preoperative checklists, environmental cleaning algorithms, and statistical process control charts. 7. Success factors for evaluation include: Focusing on measuring and improving compliance with current process measures before implementing specific interventions to address persistent SSI rates. Sharing evaluation results to educate and engage diverse perioperative teams, increasing awareness and addressing gaps in patient care processes. Providing real-time feedback and quarterly reports to keep staff informed and engaged. Offering personalized feedback to alert individual clinicians to deviations from standard practices. Conducting external reviews of implementation and evaluation processes to provide additional insights. 8. Barriers to improvement include: Relying on a single intervention (unimodal approaches) rather than a comprehensive strategy. Failing to involve multiple levels of staff or disciplines in the implementation process. Insufficient time dedicated to training and education, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Lack of direct leadership involvement to facilitate and demonstrate local culture change. Perceived or actual additional costs associated with interventions. Poor access to necessary supplies to address known risk factors. Ineffective communication and lack of awareness of the need to address the problem. Resistance to change due to previous beliefs, traditions, or misconceptions about infection control. Limited availability of data to support improvement efforts. Non-attendance or non-compliance with educational activities. 9. The Surgical Unit-based Safety Program (SUSP-Africa) was a multimodal intervention project conducted in five hospitals across Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe between July 2013 and December 2015. It combined technical measures for SSI prevention with adaptive approaches to enhance the safety climate in surgical services. 10. The project involved five phases: Preparation: Local teams identified key SSI prevention measures and prepared conditions for implementation, including tool adaptation and equipment procurement. Baseline assessment: A 10-month period of SSI surveillance and monitoring of process indicators. Intervention: Roll-out and implementation of the intervention. Follow-up assessment: A 10-month evaluation of the intervention's impact. Multimodal intervention: Integration of six technical SSI prevention measures with adaptive approaches to improve the local safety climate and motivate compliance. 11. SSI surveillance was a critical component of the SUSP approach, despite challenges in resource-limited settings. Factors supporting surveillance included: Development of a specific protocol adapted from CDC methods. Inclusion of both elective and emergency operations, with a target of 50 operations per month. 30-day follow-up after procedures using chart reviews, outpatient clinic attendance, telephone calls, and patient-submitted wound pictures. Data collection by operating room and infection prevention staff, with additional nursing staff employed to lead surveillance activities. 12. The adaptive approach aimed to improve the local safety climate by engaging leadership, identifying local champions, improving communication, and promoting accountability among frontline staff. Tools such as educational videos, posters, and discussion-oriented exercises supported these efforts. 13. Lessons learned from SUSP-Africa highlight the importance of addressing barriers to implementation early in the process, as part of the preparedness phase, to ensure the success of improvement programs.
